stories.headline: OpenAI charges only when AI works, joining new billing trend
stories.hook: New model aligns cost with successful output.
stories.tldr: OpenAI is shifting some customer billing to charge only when its AI completes tasks without human involvement. This mirrors Sierra and Fin, which Salesforce acquired for $3.6 billion on similar terms. Cognition offers up to $10 million in credits if results fail to match the price paid. CEO Marc Benioff noted that customers want varied pricing options. The move suggests a broader industry shift toward value-based metrics rather than pure compute usage.

facts.text: Sierra and Fin, the latter now being acquired by Salesforce for $3.6 billion, charge only for tasks the AI completes without human involvement.
The coding assistant Cognition promises corporate customers credits of up to $10 million if the software fails to deliver results worth at least as much as the price they paid.
Customers want to buy and price in different ways, CEO Marc Benioff said at an investor conference.

stances.position: The math finally matches the output. If the AI fails, the ledger stays empty. That is basic arithmetic.
This unlocks enterprise contracts blocked by risk aversion. When you guarantee value, you unlock budgets.
We have seen this before. Performance-based pricing was the dream of the SaaS boom. It returns when tech matures.

body.text: Sierra and Fin operate on a simple principle: charge only when the AI completes a task without human involvement. Fin is now part of Salesforce, acquired for $3.6 billion. The market validated that model. Cognition takes it further. They promise corporate customers credits of up to $10 million if the software fails to deliver results worth at least as much as the price they paid. OpenAI is now testing a similar approach. Some customers will only pay when the AI actually works. CEO Marc Benioff stated at an investor conference that customers want to buy and price in different ways. The data supports the demand for variable pricing structures. This is not magic. It is accounting.

You are witnessing the end of the pilot purgatory. For years, enterprises bought AI credits hoping for miracles. Now, the bill is tied to the miracle. This changes the procurement dynamic entirely. When a vendor like Cognition guarantees value or refunds the cost, the risk shifts from the buyer to the seller. OpenAI’s move signals that they believe their models have crossed the threshold from experimental tool to reliable worker. This is not just a billing tweak; it is a signal of confidence. Watch what happens next. Competitors will scramble to match this guarantee. The race is no longer about who has the biggest model, but who can prove it works every time. You are going to see this play out in Q4 earnings calls.

It rhymes with the early days of cloud computing, where you paid for uptime rather than raw server hours. But unlike those early days, this time the product actually has to work first. The difference is reliability. We saw this with Salesforce itself. They moved from licensing fees to subscription models based on usage and success. The pattern repeats because the underlying problem never changes: buyers want certainty, sellers want scale. The tension between them drives innovation. OpenAI is just acknowledging that the technology has finally matured enough to support this kind of contract. It is not new. It is just late.

stories.headline: Anthropic cuts cache read costs by 75% for Claude Fable and Mythos 5.1
stories.hook: Cache reads drop to $0.25 per million, but base input/output rates stay at $10 and $50.
stories.tldr: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 with a significant pricing update. Cache reads have fallen 75% to $0.25 per million, while base input and output pricing remains unchanged at $10 and $50 per million respectively. The platform reports over 2 million monthly views, indicating sustained audience interest. This adjustment targets the cost of retrieving stored context rather than altering fundamental compute costs. For teams running high-frequency inference with context reuse, this lowers marginal costs without touching core model rates.

facts.text: Cache reads fall 75% to $0.25 per million; base rates are untouched.
Base input and output pricing is unchanged at $10 and $50 per million.
The platform boasts of over 2 million monthly views, illustrating its popularity among audiences.

stances.position: Cache reads fell 75% to $0.25 per million, while base input and output pricing remained untouched at $10 and $50 per million.
The 75% drop in cache read costs unlocks efficiency for high-context workloads, even as base rates hold steady.

transcript.text: I was paged at 3 a.m. last week because someone tried to optimize a pipeline using the old cache rates. They had built their budgeting model around the previous structure, assuming the base rates were the only variable that mattered. When Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, the headline grabbed everyone’s attention, but the fine print was where the actual friction lived. The cache reads have fallen by 75%, landing at $0.25 per million. It sounds small until you realize how many times your system hits that cache during a standard session. The workaround nobody documents is simply to stop treating cache as a free layer. It used to be cheap enough to ignore; now it is cheap enough to audit.

Look at the curve. Cache reads are 75% cheaper now. That changes the math for any app that reuses long prompts. Base rates are static, sure, but the marginal cost of memory just dropped through the floor. You are going to see this shift in the way teams structure their long-context applications. The base input and output pricing is unchanged at $10 and $50 per million, so the core compute cost hasn't moved. But the 75% cut in cache read costs means that storing and retrieving context is no longer a penalty. This unlocks a different kind of efficiency. Instead of truncating history to save money, you can keep more context active without blowing the budget. The platform boasts of over 2 million monthly views, illustrating its popularity among audiences who are looking for exactly this kind of granular optimization.

You should check your own usage logs against the new $0.25 per million rate before you commit to the old architecture.
